This paper presents a method that lines these different recordings up and splits them into shared building blocks, each showing a common activity pattern and how strongly it appears in each trial and each neuron. The authors report tests on simulated data, artificial recurrent networks, monkey motor-cortex data, and 93 mouse brain-wide recordings.
summary.why: Combining recordings that do not share the same cells or trials could make large public datasets easier to compare and interpret. The text reports that one component isolated the response to silencing a motor-planning region (ALM) in mice, and that a reference from correct trials revealed inhibition-related activity on error trials; the wider significance for neuroscience is not established by this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Large-scale neural recordings increasingly span many sessions, brain regions and animals, but differences in neuronal sampling make it difficult to identify and interpret shared patterns. We introduce Neuralign, a tensor- based model that jointly aligns and decomposes recordings into components, each pairing a shared temporal pattern with its expression in individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, matched trials or behavioural labels. In simulations, pooling recordings improved recovery of shared components; in recurrent networks, Neuralign distinguished related from distinct task solutions. In the macaque motor cortex, label-free components recovered the ring-like organisation of reach directions. Across 93 brain-wide mouse recordings, Neuralign discovered a single component that isolated the response to inhibition of the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). A reference learned from correct, uninhibited trials revealed inhibition-related activity outside the choice direction on error trials, most strongly in the ALM and thalamus. Neuralign provides an interpretable framework for studying the shared structure of large neural datasets, linking shared patterns to individual trials and recorded populations.

papers.title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
papers.label: bioRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.766497 v1

summary.background:
- Neural population activity: recordings from many neurons at once, treated as a point moving through a high-dimensional space.
- Spike-train co-smoothing: predicting the activity of held-out neurons from the others, a standard benchmark task (Neural Latents Benchmark, NLB'21).
- Hyperbolic geometry: a curved space, in which tree-like or hierarchical structures are often represented more compactly than in flat space; the Poincaré ball is one model of it.
- Curvature: a number describing how strongly a space bends; positive curvature here means the Poincaré-ball model is in use with a learned scale parameter.
- State space model (S4D): a sequence model that processes time series using a set of decaying oscillatory components.
- Ring manifold: a loop-shaped pattern of population activity, often linked to motor circuits.
- Self-supervised masked prediction: training by hiding parts of the data and asking the model to fill them in.
summary.one_liner: NeuroMASS v4 is a neural network for predicting held-out spike activity on Neural Latents Benchmark recordings that embeds neural population states in a learnable hyperbolic (Poincaré ball) space and claims the learned curvature tracks circuit topology across motor and cognitive cortical datasets.
summary.plain: The paper asks whether the shape of the space that brain activity lives in can be learned from recordings of many neurons firing in monkeys. The authors build a model that takes spike counts from many neurons, predicts the missing parts of them, and learns a curved "hyperbolic" geometry along the way. They report that the learned curvature is clearly positive for two motor datasets and near zero for a frontal cognitive dataset, and they interpret this as a sign of the circuit's underlying structure.
summary.why: If learned geometry really reflects circuit organization, it could give a compact, comparable way to describe different brain areas. However, the text gives only a summary of the claim; it does not show the statistical tests, baselines, or controls behind "statistically predicts," so the strength of the evidence is hard to judge from this description alone.

papers.abstract: The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincar&eacute-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincar&eacute-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.
